explains: Every tuned number in the whole game, in one place — the battle's under 'battle', the realm's under 'court'. If a number appears in the rules and is not in this file, that is a bug; a playtest tunes exactly one file. Where the two source battle designs disagreed on a number, the entry says which was chosen and why in a 'chose' note. Battle units are strict: distances in millimetres, time in ticks (20 ticks = 1 second), angles in brads (4096 = a full turn), and the three feeling-bars — morale, cohesion, fatigue — run 0 to 1,000,000 inside the machine (divide by 1000 for the number on the page).

whereNumbersLive.explains: One rule, so nobody has to argue about it again. If a number appears in a FORMULA in the writs, or is shared by more than one table, it lives here and the tables point at it with a 'k' key. If a number is one row's own fact — a spear's reach, a formation's man-width, a seat's levers, a holding's income, one grievance's weight — it lives on that row, where a reader can see it without opening a second file. Anything else would either make this file a museum of every stat in the game or make the manual unreadable, and the manual is the acceptance test.
whereNumbersLive.kKeys: A 'k' field in another data file is a dotted path into this one. It means: the number is here, and this row is the explanation of it.
whereNumbersLive.proseDrift: Where a row's `explains` says a number out loud for a twelve-year-old, that sentence is prose and can go stale if the constant is retuned. Known, accepted, and listed in docs/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md.

time.explains: The battle is chopped into twenty slices a second and every slice does exactly the same work in exactly the same order. That is what makes a replay a replay: run it again with the same seed and the same thing happens, down to the last arrow. plannedBattleTicks is the yardstick that turns a latecomer's 'a quarter of the way through' into a tick.
time.chose: 20 ticks per second from design A; design B's 10 was rejected because the Six Seconds and courier delays are calibrated at 50 ms slices.

space.explains: The field is 1.2 kilometres wide and 800 metres deep, cut into 8-metre tiles for the ground and 32-metre cells for finding who is near whom. A brad is a slice of a circle: 4096 make a full turn, 1024 is a right angle. Computers are exact with brads and sloppy with degrees.
space.chose: Design A's field; design B's 1200 x 900 m differed only in depth and A's tile grid was already built to these numbers.

scales.explains: Morale, cohesion and fatigue run 0 to 1,000,000 inside and 0 to 1000 on the page. Chances are counted per mille — out of a thousand — so 350 means a 35 percent chance. Heed runs 0 to 100 because captains are people, not machines.

speeds.explains: Millimetres per tick. A walking man covers 65 every tick, which is 1.3 metres a second. A galloping warhorse covers 450 — nine metres a second — and that number gets SQUARED when it hits something, which is the single most important fact in the game.
speeds.chose: Courier 500 mm/tick (10 m/s) from design A over design B's 7 m/s: the nine-second ride to the far wing is a tuned feel of this field size. B's two riders — a quarter longer past danger, three seconds to find a captain in the press — were adopted on top.

acceleration.explains: Nobody starts at full speed. A horse needs 150 ticks — seven and a half seconds, about 34 metres — to reach a gallop. That is why a charge ordered from too close arrives at a trot and does almost nothing, and why the ground between the armies is the most valuable thing on the field.

turning.explains: Turning is slow and it messes up your ranks. A well-drilled unit turns faster; a unit already fighting turns at barely a third speed — which is exactly why getting round somebody's side wins battles: they cannot look at you in time.

spacing.explains: In close order each man owns about two-thirds of a square metre; in loose order well over two. That is three and a half times more space, and arrows care about nothing else. Changing between them takes four seconds during which you are neither one thing nor the other.

melee.explains: Every tick, the men who can actually reach each other take a swing. Whether it lands is 'hit'; whether it does anything through armour is 'wound'. Reach decides the first six seconds. Then the press: long weapons drop to one fighting rank, take their crowd penalty, and the reach advantage becomes half of itself as a PENALTY — computed from primary weapons even after sidearms are drawn, because the man is still tangled with his pike. Short weapons gain +12 penetration in the press, because at grappling distance you aim at the gaps in the armour. Backing out of a melee lets the enemy hit you two and a half times as hard for one tick.
melee.chose: Design A's press model whole. Design B's engagement break-off (both sides resting when ground down) was not adopted — see OPEN-QUESTIONS.

verifiedRatios.explains: The engine must reproduce these before anything else is built on top (see WRIT-THE-BATTLE, implementation order step 2).
verifiedRatios.spearNoSidearmVsSword: clash 6.6:1 to spears, press 1:1.70 to swords — an 11-fold swing
verifiedRatios.pikesVsCompanySwords: clash 1.7:1 to pikes, press 1:15.9 to swords
verifiedRatios.spearAndSwordVsSwords: clash 6.9:1, press 1:1.17 — near even. This is what a sidearm is worth.

wound.explains: Wound chance is penetration cubed against armour cubed. The cube is deliberate: it makes armour a WALL rather than a slope. A sword cut lands 976 in 1000 against a man in a shirt and 38 in 1000 against full harness — which is why armies carry hammers and mauls: high penetration crosses the wall where a sharp edge cannot.

arcs.explains: Front is the 120-degree wedge you are looking at; flank is the next 60 each side; rear is everything behind. Your mail shirt still covers your back — armour only falls to 70 percent behind you. Your shield does not — it falls to nothing. Add up armour, shields, who can swing back and the fear, and a flank attack is worth about four times a frontal one and a rear attack about eight.

shock.explains: When something moving hits something standing, the damage depends on how many men actually collide, how heavy they are, and — this is the whole design — the SQUARE of how fast they were still going at contact. Halve the speed and you quarter the damage. Braced spears have no magic bonus against horses; they take the speed away and the square does the rest.
shock.formula: shockRaw = impactMen * massPerManKg * (closingSpeed/10)^2 / 1000; kills = shockRaw * 240 / resist

worked.explains: Fifty knights, full gallop, fifteen files impacting. The swing from top to bottom is nearly three hundred to one and not one line of it is a bonus table.
worked.intoBracedLevySpearsShakenAt382: 10.4 men — the same braced spears, frightened and ragged
worked.intoBracedLevySpearsSteadyAt125: 1.0 men — and then the spears kill the stalled horses
worked.orderedFromOnly25mAt180: 4.7 men — 16 percent of a proper charge; the run-up is the weapon
worked.acrossMudAt225: 7.0 men — mud halves the speed, the square quarters the damage

shock.readOnField: Against braced points the horses visibly slow in the last twelve metres and stop. Against anyone else they do not slow at all.

refusal.explains: A horse will not run onto a set spear point. Refusal is a slowing field projected in front of a braced polearm line or planted stakes, and it is multiplied by how steady and how well-dressed that line is — frightened men with a wobbly line project almost nothing, and get ridden over, which is exactly the rule working. Men on foot feel it too, but only a quarter as strongly and over 30 percent of the distance: a man balks in the last few paces where a horse balks from twelve metres out. FRONT ARC ONLY — a braced block charged in the flank has no refusal at all, which is why pikes need horsemen on their wings.
refusal.chose: Design A whole — the graft names this the best single idea in either battle design. Design B's binary balk-at-10-metres was folded away; B's impalement story (a boastful captain pressing a refused charge) was kept as a rider in shock.

missiles.explains: Arrows are shot at a patch of ground, they FLY — three seconds to reach 150 metres — and land on whoever is standing there; a target that moved is missed, and the sim never leads the target. How many hit depends almost entirely on how tightly packed the target stands. Arrows kill slowly and frighten badly (the 1400 fear multiplier): their real job is to make the enemy breakable, and then you charge.

fatigue.explains: Wind. Running drains 560 a tick, so a fresh man is blown after about ninety seconds of running. Armour multiplies it — full harness costs about half again the wind of a padded jack. Tired men swing slower, move slower, and — the sting — their morale CEILING erodes, so they can never be fully brave again. The counter to elite heavy foot is to make it chase you.

terrain.explains: What the ground does, in numbers. Slope changes speed and wind; the sight line decides whether a unit can see the Crown Banner, which decides whether your order takes one second or nine. The per-tile ground multipliers are each ground type's own facts and live in data/terrain.json.
terrain.chose: Design A's tile grid and slope formulas whole; design B's coarse twenty-metre height grid and per-degree slope table were dropped because the integer law wants a grade in per mille, not an angle in degrees.

cohesion.explains: How well dressed the ranks are. Standing still fixes it; moving, running, turning, rough ground and being hit wreck it. A ragged unit delivers a weaker charge, braces worse, fights worse — and takes fewer arrows, because it is spread out. Cohesion is the invisible price of every manoeuvre, which is why 'just go round them' is never free. startBase and startPerPoint turn the Host's 0-100 social cohesion into a starting bar (this canon's own bridge — see OPEN-QUESTIONS).

morale.explains: Morale is the real health bar. Casualties are only the INPUT; collapse is the OUTPUT. Every pressure a unit feels adds or subtracts a little will, every tick; when it runs out the unit routs, and a routing unit sprays panic ninety metres while a steady unit steadies only forty-five — panic travels twice as far as courage, and that one asymmetry is why battles end in an avalanche, not a grind. The ceiling only ever falls. ceilingFromResolve* turn the Host's 0-100 resolve into a starting ceiling (this canon's bridge between the court's scale and the battle's — see OPEN-QUESTIONS).

command.explains: Orders do not appear in a captain's head. A rider carries them at ten metres a second and is busy for the ride out AND back; a unit that can SEE the Crown Banner takes the signal in one second instead. Couriers are the court's hand on your throat: their count IS the Host's orderCapacity — a vacant Marshalcy is two riders, a great Marshal six. Standing-plan slots at deployment are orderCapacity plus two.
command.chose: couriers = orderCapacity is the graft's join between design A's courier scarcity and the court's order capacity: two dials that turned out to be the same dial.

captains.explains: A captain rides with one of his units, which is the price of the heart he puts into the men around him. If that unit breaks he may fall with it; if it is destroyed he does. His contingent then loses its wits: no orders heeded at all for half a minute, none of his own-hand actions, and then a successor who is three-quarters the man at everything. Killing the enemy's best captain can decide a day, and so can gambling with yours.
captains.chose: Design B's mortality model whole. Design A had no captain-death rule at all, which left the Aftermath's captain fates with nothing to compute them from — a real gap, filled here.

heed.explains: When an improvised order lands, the captain weighs it once — the court's obedience for, danger and dead friends against, a seeded wobble of eight either way — and the score picks one of six outcomes. Every outcome is visible motion and every one is heralded with its cause named. Thresholds are design B's, verbatim; the score is built on the Host's obedience number so a wergild you never paid is a charge that never happens.
heed.chose: Design B's six-outcome table over design A's obey/hesitate/refuse roll: richer, and disobedience becomes motion instead of a null.

tide.explains: The Tide is each side's momentum, READ every second from the last thirty seconds of events with a fifteen-second half-life, clamped to plus or minus 25 — never stored: delete the events and the Tide is gone. Every unit's morale drifts by tide x 8 milli per tick, so winning firms an army up and losing makes it brittle. The fast decay is the anti-snowball: an early advantage evaporates unless pressed.
tide.chose: Design B whole — it is a pure reading over the event record, which is exactly this project's spine. Integer-encoded with a checked-in decay table for the integer law.
tide.decayTableNote: TIDE_DECAY[i] = round(4096 * 0.5^(i/15)) for i = 0..30, indexed by whole seconds of age; checked into source.

treachery.explains: How the battle spends the court's treachery number — the contract leaves the how to the battle, so the battle must say. Every two seconds, a contingent whose treachery is 40 or more, on a side whose Tide has sunk to -10 or worse, may act: at 60+ it DEFECTS to the enemy; at 40-59 it withdraws from the field. The chance per check is (treachery - 30) x 2 per mille. The court guarantees the player could have read the number before summoning — so when it happens it is not the game cheating, it is the game remembering.

pursuit.explains: When an army breaks the killing starts, because running men cannot defend themselves and horsemen ride them down three and a half times faster than footmen. This is where lords are captured — ransom and leverage back at court. But the longer your men chase, the deafer they get: bloodlust adds up to 250 to every future order's difficulty, and a strung-out, blown pursuit is the softest target on the field. This is exactly how you lose a battle you already won.

army.explains: An army breaks when about 45 percent of it has run or died, or its average will collapses for five seconds, or the Crown Banner falls while the day is already going badly, or every captain is down. Armies break; they are not slaughtered to the man — the slaughter comes AFTER, in the pursuit.

aftermath.explains: How the battle fills the report the court absorbs. Wounded-versus-dead tilts with the supply train's physicians; veterancy is earned by time in contact; ransoms price a captive by his standing at court.

rng.explains: The dice are fake in the best way: they come from a formula seeded by one number. Same seed, same battle, forever. Each unit gets its own private dice, so the computer can update units in any order and get exactly the same battle.
rng.streams: one global stream for army-level events; one per unit seeded from hash(battleSeed, unitIndex)

integerLaw.explains: Not one decimal number anywhere in the battle. Decimals on different machines sometimes disagree in the last digit, and a battle that disagrees in the last digit will, ten thousand ticks later, disagree about who won. Whole numbers never lie.
integerLaw.chose: Design A's law; design B used floating point and lost the argument to the replay.
integerLaw.trig: 1024-entry integer sine table scaled by 4096; 257-entry atan table

calendar.explains: The year has four seasons of ninety days. Everything in the court is counted in days, because days are the thing you never have enough of. There is no end-turn: the clock advances only when an act is placed on a track.

obligation.explains: A vassal owes forty days of fighting a year — that is the vessel. Coin instead of men is scutage, two crowns per man owed. But an obligation nobody uses starts to be forgotten: after three straight years of coin, the men owed shrink by a tenth a year, because his sons grew up never having marched for you.

actDays.explains: What each act of governance costs in DAYS off the deadline, and which track it sits on. This is the whole calendar: there is no end-turn, the clock advances only when an act is placed on a track, and you have the crown's own day-book plus one track for every filled seat. Against a forty-one-day deadline with two seats filled you have 41 crown-days and 82 officer-days, and eleven things worth doing. Coin costs are beside them where they are fixed; where they are a range, the price is read from the act itself.
actDays.chose: The court design put these on a data/acts table of its own. They are folded here instead, because they are exactly the numbers a playtest turns first and because the calendar is the game's hardest dial.

loyalty.explains: Every house starts at fifty: neither friend nor enemy. Kindness is added on and fades by half-life; grudges are taken off and do not fade — they are settled, or they cool by a fifth after ten years, and an heir inherits half. Killing a difficult lord only ever half-solves the problem.

willingness.explains: Willingness is loyalty plus the reasons he might come and minus the reasons he might not — all of it arithmetic you can do before you send the letter. There are no dice in the muster. If you can read, you can predict.

resolveFormula.explains: Resolve is how willing these men are to die for you — the most political number in the game, and it rides straight into the battle where you will feel it as a morale ceiling.

obedienceFormula.explains: Obedience is whether they will actually do what you tell them mid-battle — it feeds the heed score directly. This is where a seat you never granted turns into a tactic that never happens.

treacheryFormula.explains: Treachery is the chance he turns his coat. Holding his heir at your court takes thirty points straight off — that is what hostages are for, and why they were normal.

march.explains: Foot walks eight leagues a day on a good summer road; horse twelve; a messenger twenty-five. Calling a lord sixty-six leagues out costs four days for the letter, five to gather, six to ride — fifteen days before he stands anywhere. Distance is arithmetic, not a pathfind.

wear.explains: Every day on the road tires men; resting at the muster gives eight points back a day — but resting eats grain and burns deadline days, so it is a trade like everything else.

supply.explains: A hundred men eat one sack of grain a day. That single line decides whether you can wait for latecomers, whether you can besiege anything, and whether you are allowed to refuse a battle.

coin.explains: Your household costs three crowns a man a season, forever. Mercenaries cost two to hire and four a season after. Scutage brings two crowns per man owed — so turning a vassal's money back into soldiers costs about three times what he paid. That gap is the whole lesson of scutage.

seats.explains: A seat's power is its base strength times how good the holder is times how loyal — never below half, so a seat is never worse than empty, only wasted. Hold it eight years and taking it back is a serious insult; sixteen and everyone treats it as the house's property.

regeneration.explains: A holding replaces six men a year no matter its size — additive on purpose, so being small does not also mean recovering slowly. One of the ladders out of a losing streak.

battleJoins.explains: The numbers the court computes specifically for the battle's hands. Order capacity is the Marshal made mechanical: it becomes the battle's courier count and (plus two) its standing-plan slots. Blood-debt is only earned for losses far WORSE than everyone else's — a house that bled alongside the rest has no claim.
